chapter: Critics, the clarinet's decline and the 1950s
title: A double bill with Bill Haley and the Comets
summary: In Philadelphia he found himself opening for Bill Haley and the Comets.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: So, let’s rewind a tiny bit and talk about rock and roll . . .
Rock and roll.
For a second again.
[laughter]
And you actually had a double-bill with Bill Haley and the Comets?

Yeah, that was a strange situation. I played; it was at a club, famous club in Philadelphia. In fact, the owner at that time was married to Barbara Walters. And, usually we were booked with other jazz groups that I was familiar with, one time I played opposite Oscar’s group. This time I had another group I’d never heard of and I played my set, I came off stage, and then this other group followed me and I thought it was a joke. And I said . . .
[laughter] Jokes on you!

[laughter] Yeah, jokes on me! I said to the owner, “what in the world? What in the world.” He said, “I hate to tell you this, but they’re going to get billing over you for the rest of the two weeks because the people are coming to hear them, not your group.” He was that straight forward about it.

And this was a venue that usually presented jazz? I mean, you think of an audience that is used to patronizing a certain venue and it seems like the audience for you and the audience for Bill Haley and the Comets . . .
Yeah, it turned out to be Bill Haley and the Comets.
Amazing.

And, it got so that by mid week of the first week the audience couldn’t wait for us to get off the stage so they could hear this other group, and it didn’t make much sense to me, but it sure did with the public.
And that was 1955, I think.
Yeah, somewhere in there. What they said was true, they put Billy’s name up there. I was second to Billy…Lee somebody was the owner.
This was Barbara Walter’s husband.
Yeah, husband. He had quite a lot of . . . he was pretty well known and pretty wealthy guy, a lot of holdings in Philadelphia and elsewhere.
Well, so these Rock and Rollers, they moved in on all the, all the jazz players.
Kind of, yeah, yeah.
So, those were tough times for a lot of people.
Of course.
